summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people, and the sources reviewed document no trans-specific violence against a visitor: no assault, mob attack or police-brutality case involving a trans traveller is recorded. The hate-crime material below is aggregate national reporting, not an incident series involving visitors.

Police recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences, the highest total ever logged, with defamation and assault the most common types. The Police University College reports the sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category climbing across six reported years, from 72 cases to 241. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 gives the same headline total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes and identifies sexual orientation and gender identity as recurrent motives, present in 12% of cases.

The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence. Motive is captured only in police reports, so sexual-orientation and gender-identity-motivated incidents are counted as reported suspicions rather than as charges, and the recorded figures measure reporting behaviour as much as offending.

Finland's first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault, with convictions in March. Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices by 125 votes to 49 in March, while a full statutory ban remained pending at the time of the review.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since 1 March 2017. Since 28 February 2018 the Maternity Act recognises both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of the child's birth, with the second parent registered at birth rather than through adoption.
tangentialFactors:
Finland's authorities issue outbound travel guidance to their own transgender citizens rather than assessments of conditions at home. In March 2025 Finland updated its advice for transgender people travelling to the United States following that country's 'two genders' executive order; another Nordic state issued parallel advice telling trans travellers to contact the destination country's embassy before departure over document problems. The guidance concerns risk in a third country and says nothing about risk inside Finland.

The 2017 marriage law was produced by the citizens' initiative route. The 'Tahdon2013' campaign collected more than 162,000 certified signatures, the largest Finnish initiative ever and far above the 50,000 threshold that forces parliamentary consideration, against an organiser target of 250,000.

Take-up after legal change was immediate: a single provincial register office had about 41 same-sex couples scheduled to marry in the first week of marriage equality. This is one register office, not a national rate.

Finland is one of six countries examined in which infertility requirements were written explicitly into legal gender recognition law, alongside the Netherlands and Sweden. At least 11,000 people were subjected to such conditions across the six countries, with Sweden legislating first in 1972 and keeping the requirement in force for 40 years.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in Finland was conditioned on a statutory infertility requirement for decades. The last such requirement was phased out at the end of June 2025, so the sterilisation-era rule no longer applies, but the cohort subjected to it is documented and its effects are not reversible.

Resident-facing protection against conversion practices rests on a pending law rather than an in-force ban. The citizens' initiative cleared its parliamentary endorsement in March by 125 to 49, and the first prosecution proceeded under assault provisions rather than under a dedicated conversion-practices offence.

Hate-crime protection for residents is evidentiary rather than statutory. Because the Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, motive is recorded at the reporting stage and can only influence later charging and sentencing through the police file.
outOfScopeNotes:
The two sources give the same total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes but attribute it to different years, 2024 in the Police University College release and 2025 in the ILGA-Europe review. The discrepancy is unresolved in the sources reviewed and neither document reconciles it.

Restroom and facility rules, gender-marker changes on identity documents, entry and visa screening, and access to gender-affirming care for short-term visitors are not addressed in the sources reviewed for this revision.

The status of a full statutory ban on conversion practices is unresolved: the citizens' initiative was endorsed in March but the review states a complete ban remained pending, with no later enactment sourced here.

No source in the inventory reports an incident count for hate crimes against foreign visitors specifically; the 1,808 figure is not disaggregated by victim residency or nationality.
